![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/bd504e1d8d85a2f2bbb4b75bd6825120a6aef15345c704714931b6270f84796f.png)

 

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle 0, \: 0, \: 1 + xyz \rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$
current_example.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $\mathbf F =  \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1+xyz\rangle$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/977d93ad65c9f3690def4242f98f4de5e5c89faf02fe47d06f5ed251d8a4a292.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ through these two sides.

- Let $S_1$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z = 1$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_1$ is

$$
\mathbf n_1 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 1$ on $S_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =1+xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}1+xy\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}1+xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}1+xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+\frac{1}{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Let $S_2$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $S_2$ is

$$
\mathbf n_2 = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z = 0$ on $S_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,1+xyz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S_2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =-\text{Area}(D) \\  & =-(1-0)(1-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+(-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
